What is a magnetic storm?

A magnetic storm is a disturbance of the Earth's magnetic field. It is caused by the solar wind and by plasma ejections from the Sun (CMEs). When such a cloud reaches the Earth, its magnetic field is “shaken”. This can affect satellites, GPS and radio links, and in strong storms the aurora can be seen far to the south.

What does the Kp index mean?

The Kp index shows how disturbed the Earth's magnetic field is, on a scale from 0 to 9:

KpLevelWhat it means
0–3CalmNormal conditions
4ActiveIncreased activity, not a storm
5G1 — minor stormAurora in northern Scandinavia
6G2 — moderate stormAurora in southern Scandinavia
7G3 — strong stormAurora in northern Europe
8G4 — severe stormAurora in central Europe
9G5 — extreme stormAurora may be visible even in Bulgaria

How is the forecast made?

The forecast comes from the NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center, the US space weather service. The SOHO and STEREO satellites photograph the Sun and detect plasma ejections. The DSCOVR satellite, 1.5 million km from the Earth towards the Sun, measures the solar wind 30–60 minutes before it reaches us. A computer model calculates when the cloud will arrive, and forecasters issue the 3-day Kp forecast. It is good for today and tomorrow and indicative for the third day, because the arrival time is uncertain by about ±7–12 hours.

Do magnetic storms affect health?

Research shows no clear effect on most people. Some weather-sensitive people report headaches, fatigue or poor sleep on storm days. If you have health complaints, consult a doctor.

Can the aurora be seen in Bulgaria?

Rarely, only in extreme storms with Kp 8–9. That happened in May 2024, when the aurora was seen across Bulgaria low above the northern horizon.
